Every figure in the forest, drawn with `geom-viz` from the very objects the
note is about. Each one also sits inside its own note; this page is the contact
sheet, so you can see them all without hunting. There are fifteen drawings:
thirteen are built from a `geom-viz` scene, and two — the conformal embedding
and the three cases of the exponential — are page-space diagrams drawn with the
same renderer.

## The geometric product and a rotor

For vectors $u$ and $v$, the geometric product splits as

```typst
u v = u dot v + u and v,
```

where $u dot v$ is the scalar (dot) product and $u and v$ is the bivector: the
oriented parallelogram they span. A rotor $R$ acts on a vector $x$ by the
sandwich $x |-> R x tilde(R)$. See [[191286d7|the Euclidean algebra]].

## Blades of every grade

Three vectors $u, v, w$ in `Cl(3,0,0)` span a line (grade 1, $u$), a plane
(grade 2, $u and v$) and a volume (grade 3, $u and v and w$). See [[ad136f1c|A blade is a subspace with a magnitude]].

<figcaption style="text-align:center;font-size:0.85em;opacity:0.7;margin-top:0.4em">The three grades in the Euclidean algebra: a vector u (grade 1), the parallelogram u and v (grade 2), and the parallelepiped u and v and w (grade 3). Each grade adds one dimension of span.</figcaption>
</figure>

## The contraction is a quarter turn

For the orthonormal basis vectors $e_1, e_2$ and the plane $e_12 = e_1 and e_2$,
the left contraction satisfies $e_1 dot e_12 = e_2$ and
$e_2 dot e_12 = -e_1$. See [[f7e286b8|The left contraction is the metric projection]].

<figcaption style="text-align:center;font-size:0.85em;opacity:0.7;margin-top:0.4em">The contraction is a quarter turn in the plane: contracting e1 with the plane e12 gives e2, and contracting e2 with it gives -e1.</figcaption>
</figure>

## The Hodge dual

In `Cl(3,0,0)` the pseudoscalar is $I = e_123$ and the right dual is
$B^* = B I^(-1)$. For the plane $B = e_12$ this gives the normal vector
$B^* = e_3$. See [[d32870e7|The Hodge dual trades a blade for its complement]].

## Incidence in PGA

Three planes $pi_1, pi_2, pi_3$ in `Cl(3,0,1)`; the meet of the first two is
their line $l = pi_1 and pi_2$, and the meet of all three is the point
$p = pi_1 and pi_2 and pi_3$. Every incidence is a wedge. See
[[1d71e490|meet and join in PGA]].

<figcaption style="text-align:center;font-size:0.85em;opacity:0.7;margin-top:0.4em">Three planes, the line where two of them meet, and the point where the third cuts that line. Every incidence here is a wedge.</figcaption>

## Four conformal constructions

With $X_i$ conformal points and $e_oo$ the point at infinity: two points give
the point pair $X_1 and X_2$, three give the circle
$(X_1 and X_2 and X_3)^*$, four give the sphere
$(X_1 and X_2 and X_3 and X_4)^*$, and three points plus $e_oo$ give the plane
$(X_1 and X_2 and X_3 and e_oo)^*$. See
[[5d4f04c6|the construction recipe]].

<figcaption style="text-align:center;font-size:0.85em;opacity:0.7;margin-top:0.4em">The four constructions side by side: two points give a point pair, three a circle, four a sphere, and three points plus e-infinity a plane. In each panel the points are the input and the object is the dual of their wedge.</figcaption>
</figure>

## Wedge the points, then dualise

Three conformal points $X_1, X_2, X_3$ span a triangle; the direct blade
$X_1 and X_2 and X_3$ is their projective span, and its dual $z$ is the
circumcircle. See [[5d4f04c6|the construction recipe]].

## Round versus flat

A sphere $S$ and a plane $pi$; the contraction with the point at infinity gives
$e_oo dot S = -1$ for the round object and $e_oo dot pi = 0$ for the flat one.
See [[86c369c2|Round versus flat: the e∞ contraction decides]].

<figcaption style="text-align:center;font-size:0.85em;opacity:0.7;margin-top:0.4em">Round versus flat: a sphere has e-infinity dot S = -1, a plane has e-infinity dot pi = 0. The single contraction with the point at infinity decides the family.</figcaption>
</figure>

## A transversion bends space

A transversion with parameter vector $bold(a)$ is generated by the null
bivector $-a_i e_i and e_0$; it is conformal, so angles survive and only the
scale varies. See [[649e54f0|A transversion bends space without moving infinity]].

## ScLERP along a screw

Five frames along the group exponential
$M(lambda) = M_0 exp(lambda log(M_0^(-1) M_1))$, and the screw axis they all
share. See [[0248bd6b|screw interpolation]].

</figure>

## The conformal embedding of a line

The coordinate $x$ becomes the conformal point
$X = x + 1 slash 2 x^2 e_oo + e_0$ on a parabola, where $e_0$ and $e_oo$ are
the two null basis vectors of `Cl(4,1)`; the chord $X and Y$ encodes the
distance between the two points. See [[50ea1633|the embedding note]].

## Three cases of the exponential

A simple bivector $B$ satisfies one of $B^2 < 0$, $B^2 > 0$ or $B^2 = 0$; the
exponential is respectively a rotation, a boost and a translation. See
[[0aa35a84|Exponentiating a simple bivector closes in three cases]].

<svg role="img" aria-label="The three geometries of one plane. <figcaption style="text-align:center;font-size:0.85em;opacity:0.7;margin-top:0.4em">The three geometries of one plane. A negative square gives a rotation, a positive square a boost (a dilation), and a zero square a translation: the three cases of the bivector exponential.</figcaption>
</figure>

## One sandwich, every object

A single motor $M$ acts on a point, a sphere, a circle, a line segment and a
plane by $X |-> M X tilde(M)$; dashed shapes are before, solid shapes are
after. See [[dc7fd3f4|The sandwich is an algebra automorphism]].
